title: Kavanah, intention
hook: Jewish prayer asks for kavanah, the heart aimed at what the lips are saying

segments.voice: Yesterday, alone in the field: Rebbe Nachman's hitbodedut, speaking to God in your own words, out loud, somewhere quiet. Your line was my own words. Did any of yours get said aloud? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-two.

The Mishnah, the collection of early Jewish law, describes a group it calls the pious ones of old. Before they prayed, it says, they would wait an hour. Not to get the words ready. They knew the words. They waited to get the heart ready, to direct it toward their Father in heaven. Then the same passage turns strict. Once you've begun, even if a king greets you, don't answer him. Even if a snake is wound around your heel, don't stop. That's a great deal of attention for a few minutes of words. Today's word is the name for what all that waiting was for.
screen: `THEY WAITED AN HOUR.` → `TO GET THE HEART READY.` → `NOT EVEN FOR A KING.`

segments.voice: The word is kavanah. It's usually translated intention, or directed intention: the heart aimed, the way you aim your steps down a road. The Mishnah uses this language of aiming the heart; in one rule about reciting the Shema, the question is simply whether a person directed his heart. The roots reach back into the Torah. Deuteronomy, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, asks Israel "to serve Him with all your heart and with all your soul." The rabbis of the Talmud asked a sharp question about that line: what kind of service happens in the heart? Their answer was prayer. So prayer is the service of the heart, and kavanah is what makes it the heart's. Then comes a tension Jewish teachers have turned over for a long time. Jewish prayer has fixed words, said at fixed times. The fixed part has its own name, keva. Kavanah is the living part. Lean only on keva and the words can run on autopilot. Wait only for kavanah and a person might never get around to praying. The Mishnah names the danger in a single line: whoever makes their prayer a fixed task, their prayer is not a plea. Notice what the tradition does with that. It doesn't throw out the fixed words because the heart wanders. It keeps the words, and keeps asking for the aim. And the idea reaches past prayer. Jewish teachers speak of kavanah in eating, in giving, in the small commanded acts of an ordinary day. The same act can be done with the heart pointed at it, or done on the way to something else.
screen: `KAVANAH: THE HEART, AIMED.` · `PRAYER, THE SERVICE OF THE HEART.` · `FIXED WORDS, LIVING AIM.` · `NOT ONLY IN PRAYER.` · then, large: `TO SERVE HIM WITH ALL YOUR HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one act with full intention. Pick something small you can do right now: a sip of water, folding your hands, standing up from your chair. Before you do it, stop. Wait one breath, the way the pious ones waited. Know what you're about to do, and why. If you pray, you can point the act toward God. If you don't, point it toward the person or the day it serves. Then do it slowly, all the way through, and nothing else. Then sit, and let each breath that follows be done the same way. The bell holds the time.
Kavanah. Directed intention: the heart aimed at what the lips or hands are doing, in Jewish prayer and beyond it. Today's word.

Your line: kavanah. Today, choose one thing you usually do on autopilot, a greeting, a meal, a doorway you walk through, and before it, wait one breath and aim. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: Jews who pray the set daily prayers try to bring kavanah, directed intention, to the fixed words; teachers in the tradition also speak of bringing it to blessings, meals and other daily acts.

myth: kavanah means throwing out the fixed words of prayer
the tradition keeps the fixed words, keva, and asks for the aim of the heart inside them.
the Mishnah says not to stop praying even for a snake around your heel
even if a king greets you, don't answer; even if a snake is wound around your heel, don't stop.
the rabbis read "serve Him with all your heart" as being about prayer
they asked what service happens in the heart, and answered: prayer.

fork.setup: you're in the middle of the fixed prayer. a king walks up and greets you. what does the Mishnah say to do?
options: answer him politely, then go back to praying.
stop, and start the whole prayer over.
fork.reveal: the Mishnah says even a king's greeting shouldn't break the prayer, and not even a snake at your heel. that's how seriously it takes the aim of the heart.

original.note: Hebrew: intention, the heart directed toward what you are doing.

trapdoor: what you thought: kavanah just means meaning it.
what it means: directed intention, the heart aimed at the act, held together with the fixed words of prayer rather than replacing them.
what a scholar hears: the Mishnah sets a fixed task against a real plea, and the Talmud reads "serve Him with all your heart" as prayer, the service of the heart.

sources.quoted: to serve Him with all your heart and with all your soul

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Deuteronomy 11:13: 'to serve Him with all your heart and with all your soul'. The script names the translation as 'the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation'; that year is the translation's name, not a claim about the text.

Mishnah Berakhot 5:1 paraphrased: the pious ones of old (chasidim harishonim) waited an hour to direct their hearts to their Father in heaven; even a king's greeting or a snake wound around the heel should not interrupt. The Talmud (Berakhot 32b-33a) limits the king case (e.g. a non-Jewish king, where there is danger); the script does not go into this. Confirm the fork's simplification is acceptable.
Mishnah Berakhot 2:1 (one reading the Torah when the time for the Shema arrives: 'if he directed his heart, he has fulfilled his obligation') is summarized loosely; confirm.
Taanit 2a: 'what is service of the heart? this is prayer' (on Deuteronomy 11:13), paraphrased.
Mishnah Berakhot 4:4 (Rabbi Eliezer: one who makes his prayer keva, his prayer is not supplication) paraphrased as 'a fixed task ... not a plea'; confirm.
Kavanah in eating, giving and mitzvot is stated generally as something 'Jewish teachers speak of'; the halakhic debate on whether mitzvot require intention (mitzvot tzrichot kavanah) is not entered.
